cards.abstract_phrase: It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes.
cards.plain_english: It's an example of a rule the argument requires.
cards.example_stimulus: Despite a high-paying job, John was stressed and depressed. Money alone doesn't make you happy.
cards.y_concrete: Money alone doesn't make you happy (the required principle)

cards.abstract_phrase: Concludes X on the basis of Y.
cards.plain_english: Y is the support. X is the conclusion. 'On the basis of' points backward to evidence.
cards.example_stimulus: We should not approve the merger because it would reduce competition in three markets.
cards.x_concrete: We should not approve the merger (conclusion)
cards.y_concrete: It would reduce competition in three markets (evidence)

cards.abstract_phrase: Treats the occurrence of X as corroborating evidence for Y.
cards.plain_english: X happened, and the author uses it as a reason to believe Y.
cards.example_stimulus: The flu vaccine reduces hospitalizations. Hospitalizations dropped 30% in vaccinated counties last winter.

cards.abstract_phrase: Challenges the plausibility of X by offering Y as an alternative explanation.
cards.plain_english: X is a proposed cause. The author attacks X by proposing a different cause Y for the same effect.
cards.example_stimulus: The vase didn't break because of the earthquake. It was already cracked, and the cleaner brushed against it.
cards.x_concrete: The earthquake broke the vase (the challenged cause)
cards.y_concrete: A prior crack plus a brush from the cleaner (alternative cause)

cards.abstract_phrase: Substantiates the claim that X is false by demonstrating that Y is an inevitable consequence of X.
cards.plain_english: If X were true, Y would have to follow. Y is unacceptable, so X is false.
cards.example_stimulus: If the suspect were in town that night, his car would have been on the bridge cameras. It wasn't. He wasn't in town.
cards.x_concrete: The suspect was in town (the claim shown false)
cards.y_concrete: His car on the bridge cameras (the missing consequence)

cards.abstract_phrase: A phenomenon for which the conclusion is offered as an explanation.
cards.plain_english: An effect that the conclusion proposes a cause for.
cards.example_stimulus: Sales dropped 12% last quarter. The likely cause is the new return policy.
cards.y_concrete: The new return policy (the proposed explanation/cause)

cards.abstract_phrase: Infers, on the grounds that X, that Y.
cards.plain_english: X is the evidence. Y is the conclusion. 'On the grounds that' points backward.
cards.example_stimulus: The fossil bed contains marine shells. This region was once underwater.
cards.x_concrete: The fossil bed contains marine shells (evidence)

cards.plain_english: X is the broader move. Y is the specific tactic that accomplishes it.
cards.example_stimulus: The author defends the policy by citing three case studies in which it worked.
cards.x_concrete: Defending the policy (X, the broader move)
cards.y_concrete: Citing three case studies (Y, the specific tactic)

cards.abstract_phrase: Presumes, without providing justification, that a condition necessary for an outcome is also sufficient to produce that outcome.
cards.example_stimulus: To win the lottery you need a ticket. I have a ticket. I will win.
cards.y_concrete: Winning the lottery (the outcome wrongly presumed guaranteed)

cards.abstract_phrase: Mistakes a temporal relationship between two events for a causal relationship.
cards.plain_english: Y came after X, so the author thinks X caused Y.
cards.example_stimulus: The rooster crowed and then the sun came up. The rooster caused the sunrise.
cards.y_concrete: The sun rising (the later event wrongly attributed to it)

cards.abstract_phrase: Rejects a position on the grounds that the proponents of the position have a vested interest in its acceptance.
cards.plain_english: Attacks the motive of the speaker instead of the speaker's argument. Ad hominem.
cards.example_stimulus: The mechanic says my brakes need replacing, but he profits from the repair, so my brakes are fine.
cards.x_concrete: The mechanic's claim that the brakes need replacing (rejected position)
cards.y_concrete: The mechanic's financial interest (the irrelevant attack)

cards.abstract_phrase: Appeals to a general principle in order to justify a particular case.
cards.plain_english: The author cites a broad rule to defend a specific decision.
cards.example_stimulus: Public officials must disclose conflicts of interest. The mayor owns shares in the firm bidding on the contract, so she must recuse herself.
cards.y_concrete: The mayor's recusal (the particular case justified)

cards.abstract_phrase: Generalizes from a small or unrepresentative sample.
cards.plain_english: The author draws a sweeping conclusion from too few or too narrow a sample.
cards.example_stimulus: Two friends quit caffeine and slept better. Quitting caffeine improves sleep for everyone.
cards.x_concrete: Two friends slept better (the unrepresentative sample)
cards.y_concrete: Quitting caffeine improves sleep universally (the overreach)

cards.abstract_phrase: Anticipates an objection and addresses it before continuing.
cards.plain_english: The author flags a possible counter-argument and shuts it down preemptively.
cards.example_stimulus: Some might object that the program is too costly, but the long-term savings exceed the upfront expense.
cards.x_concrete: The objection that the program is too costly
cards.y_concrete: The long-term savings response that addresses it

cards.abstract_phrase: Derives a conclusion about what is possible from premises about what is necessary.
cards.plain_english: Reasons from a must-be-true premise to a could-be-true conclusion.
cards.example_stimulus: Every passing student turned in the final. The student who didn't turn in the final could not have passed.
cards.x_concrete: The necessity (passing requires turning in the final)
cards.y_concrete: The possibility eliminated (the missing student cannot have passed)

cards.abstract_phrase: Posits a single cause for a phenomenon that likely has multiple contributing factors.
cards.plain_english: The author proposes one cause when the effect probably has many contributors.
cards.example_stimulus: Test scores dropped after the curriculum change. The new curriculum caused the drop.
cards.x_concrete: The drop in test scores (the phenomenon)
cards.y_concrete: The new curriculum (the single posited cause)

cards.abstract_phrase: Takes for granted that the conditions sufficient for X have actually been met.
cards.plain_english: Assumes without proof that the requirements for X are satisfied.
cards.example_stimulus: If the bill passes the Senate, it becomes law. The bill will become law.
cards.x_concrete: The bill becoming law (the assumed outcome)
cards.y_concrete: Passage in the Senate (the assumed-but-unproven condition)

cards.abstract_phrase: Undermines a claim by calling into question the sufficiency of the evidence offered for it.
cards.plain_english: Attacks a claim by showing the support is not enough to prove it.
cards.example_stimulus: Two satisfied customers is not enough to conclude the product is reliable.
cards.y_concrete: Two satisfied customers (the insufficient evidence pointed out)
